paper_title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language-model agents increasingly turn naturallanguage requests into sequences of tool calls, and compact models now make this feasible on device, within tight latency, privacy, and compute budgets (Liu et al., 2024). Such agents must obey domain policies, satisfy state-dependent preconditions, and preserve user intent across multi-step interactions, and current evaluations show that they often fail. Agents follow domain policies inconsistently (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2026), strug- *Equal Contribution gle with state dependencies and missing information (Lu et al., 2025), and execute unsafe actions when untrusted tool outputs steer their reasoning (Debenedetti et al., 2024). These failures matter most when tool call changes external state (sending message, changing reservation, initiating payment), because call that succeeds can still be transition the policy forbids. We study whether formal verification can both enforce policy-compliant behavior and help agents achieve it. We write agent policies in Lean 4 (Moura and Ullrich, 2021) and place verifier be1 tween the language model and its tools, so that an action executes only if its policy obligations are met (Figure 1). Prior work enforces symbolic or formally specified policies at runtime (Shi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Palumbo et al., 2026) and has begun to use Lean to verify agents (Rashie and Rashi, 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). We add decision procedure proved correct against an independent temporal semantics, and two ways to correct denied call: the model can fix the call from LEANGUARDs feedback, or Lean can compute fix and prove it admissible without the model. Our contributions are: LEANGUARD, Lean 4 runtime whose admission procedure is proved equivalent to temporal-logic semantics (2). On τ 2-bench, unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, and LEANGUARD executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, it reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%. Proof-guided repair (2.6). Lean metaprogramming searches for nearby call that preserves the users intent and returns it with kernelchecked proof of admissibility, without involving the model. To our knowledge, no existing agent guardrail produces proved repairs. On replayed τ 2-bench denials, it repairs 88 of the 252 denials caused by argument values, in median of 2 ms. Feedback-guided recovery (2.5). Returning feedback, the violated rule and hint, instead of bare denial, reduces repeated blocked calls, increases recovered actions from 34 to 48, and raises task success for four of five models. taxonomy and measurement of policyviolating tool calls by compact agents, in five categories that each map to part of LEANGUARD.

sections.title: 2.1 Overview
sections.content: We study language-model agents that act on stateful environment through tools, proposing actions such as modifying an order, issuing refund, or changing an account. Whether such an action is permitted is different question from whether it is well-formed, because the answer may depend on the backend state, earlier actions, what the user has been shown, prior authorization, or whether the operation was already attempted. We therefore treat guardrailing as control over state transitions. 2 The language model proposes an action, and separate policy runtime decides whether the transition is admissible under formal specification. LEANGUARD is such runtime, implemented in Lean 4. Figure 2 follows the exchange of Figure 1 through its three steps, which structure this section. The agent proposes call, which LEANGUARD grounds in trusted evidence (2.2). LEANGUARD evaluates the call against compiled Lean policies (2.3) and admits it only if the policy allows it, with proved guarantee (2.4). denied call can then be corrected by the model from LEANGUARDs feedback (2.5) or repaired by Lean with proof (2.6). Section 2.7 instantiates LEANGUARD on our two benchmarks.

sections.title: Evidence
sections.content: LEANGUARD adds no new action language. The model sees the environments ordinary tool schemas and emits an ordinary structured tool call. The host intercepts the call before it reaches the tool and treats it as untrusted data; the agent never writes Lean code, proofs, policy rules, or approval records. Before admission, the domain adapter snapshots the authoritative backend, validates the arguments, and derives the facts the policy needs. Each snapshot carries revision covering the state on which authorization depends, and past outcomes keep the facts recorded at dispatch. The model therefore cannot satisfy policy by asserting, as the injected note in Figure 2 does, that the customer has already approved. Admission is part of monitored protocol. An admitted call is recorded as dispatch reservation before the tool runs, so single-use operation cannot be repeated while its outcome is unknown. User confirmation is likewise trusted evidence, bound to the exact proposal and state revision and usable once (Appendix A).

sections.title: 2.3 Step 2: Lean Policies
sections.content: are Predicates. Predicates domain-specific checks over the decision context: the proposed tool and its arguments, facts from the environment, the relevant user or resource, and structured In Figure 2, information from the history. retail.order_owner checks the order belongs to the authenticated customer. Predicates are ordinary Lean definitions, so the runtime executes them directly and we can prove theorems about the same code. that Figure 2: LEANGUARD on the exchange of Figure 1. (1) The agent proposes call; text in tool outputs is not evidence. (2) LEANGUARD checks the call against trusted evidence, backend snapshot and the journal of earlier events, using compiled Lean rules. (3) denial returns the failed rules and hint. After the customer confirms on trusted screen, the reissued call is admitted, dispatched once, and recorded in the journal. The proved repair in (3) is computed offline by the search of 2.6; in our experiments, the agent receives only the rules and the hint. Temporal operators and scopes. Many policies cannot be expressed over the current state alone. write may be allowed only after the agent has read the resource, and mutation may be allowed at most once even if the agent retries after an uncertain response. LEANGUARD expresses such dependencies with three past-time operators over the monitored history: PREVIOUS (the property held at the preceding relevant event), ONCE (a matching event occurred earlier), and SINCE (a condition has held continuously since an earlier witnessing event). Each operator can be restricted to time window, and can be evaluated over the events that share principal, conversation, or resource, so that the previous observation of this order refers to that order and not to whatever event happened last. Rules. policy attaches three kinds of rules to tool actions: permits, requirements, and forbids. permit marks an action as belonging to an authorized class; without satisfied permit, the action is denied by default. requirement adds an obligation that must also hold whenever it applies. In Figure 2, retail.confirmation requires that the customer confirmed this exact exchange. forbid blocks an action outright; in DTap, for instance, forbid rejects operations for which the application offers no authorization path, while the τ 2-bench policies express all of their prohibitions as requirements. broad permit cannot override an unmet requirement or an applicable forbid, so authorization composes. Fail-closed evaluation. Predicates may read structured data, such as an order status or an amount, and evaluation fails if that data is missing or malformed. LEANGUARD distinguishes such an error from predicate that evaluates to false and admits an action only if every relevant component evaluates without error, so missing evidence cannot become an authorization through negation or disjunction. Semantics and verification. The executable evaluator is not the specification. We give the policy language an independent semantics in LeanLTL (Vin et al., 2025), Lean library for linear temporal logic, by embedding the history as trace that runs from the newest event to the oldest (Appendix B). We prove, for every history, that the evaluator returns true exactly when the history satisfies this interpretation, first for single temporal formulas, then for authorization, and finally for the complete admission decision with its fail-closed error condition. All proofs are checked when the policy is built, so none is constructed per tool call, and 3 verification script rejects any exported theorem that depends on sorry or another nonstandard axiom.

sections.title: 2.5 Step 3a: Feedback-Guided Recovery
sections.content: A denial need not end the attempt. With feedback, LEANGUARD returns two things to the agent. The formal part is the decision record: the identifiers of the failed rules, with the failed requirements, applicable forbids, evaluation errors, and supporting evidence. The informal part is hint that renders the failed obligation in natural language, such as ask the customer to confirm the exchange in Figure 2. The Lean policy determines the formal part; the hint only renders it and is not itself verified. The model itself must then fix the call. Section 3 compares feedback with bare denial that only says the call was not executed.

For example, if an account has spent 60 units of 100-unit budget, proposed spend of 70 can be repaired to 40 when the task allows smaller amount. Search by metaprogramming. The search is Lean tactic, guard_repair?, written with Leans metaprogramming framework. It tries the candidates in order and discharges each goal with guard_solve, which combines evaluation of concrete predicates with the arithmetic, equality reasoning, and lemma instantiation of Leans grind engine. repair is returned only together with kernel-checked proof that the policy admits it, and invalid edits are rejected by the same checker that verifies the policy. Extensibility. Because the search, the policy, and its proofs live in one language, extending repair requires no change to the runtime. Scope. repair proof holds only for the context in which it was found, so the repaired call still passes through ordinary admission, and failing to find repair in Ct does not show that none exists. The runtime does not yet call the search; we evaluate it on replayed denials (3). Instantiation on τ 2-bench and DTap 2.7 τ 2-bench. Each domain of τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2026) gives the agent natural-language policy, which we call the benchmark policy. We formalize the tool-enforceable subset of the benchmark policies of the retail, airline, and telecom domains as Lean policies. An authoring skill drafts candidate LEANGUARD definitions from the policy text, and the predicates and rules are reviewed and corrected by hand. Autoformalization is thus an offline aid, and the reviewed policy is fixed for the whole experiment. The three policies comprise 45 rules over the 43 agent tools in 583 lines of Lean (Appendix D). Two rules, retail.modify_once and stable_identity, are stricter than the benchmark policy; Section 3 counts the calls they stop separately. DTap. For DTap, single policy template is instantiated for each application with reviewed contracts for its tools, 199 across the seven domains we evaluate. contract fixes the argument schema and the resource effects of call, such as reading record or placing trade. Every effect must be covered by an exact grant from the applications trusted control plane, and sensitive writes also need an independent review of the payload and fresh, single-use confirmation (Appendix D). In our experiments, the session holds grants to read the customers own records and public data, and no write grants, reviews, or confirmations; we call this deployment read-only. Evaluation protocol. LEANGUARD never consults the benchmarks reference solution or scoring assertions; the adapter builds each context from the live benchmark database and the history so far. Task completion (the benchmark reward) and policy compliance (LEANGUARDs verdicts) are therefore measured separately.

Without feedback, agents often retry the same call. In the LEANGUARD arm, Qwen3.5-2B issues 271 blocked calls for 141 distinct denied actions, about 1.9 attempts per action  (Table 2)  . With feedback, it issues 144 blocked calls for 104 actions (1.4 per action), and over all models, blocked calls drop from 983 to 719. When the missing requirement can be met, for example by looking up the user or obtaining confirmation, agents with feedback more often meet it and reissue the call. The replay reproduces all 7,720 admission decisions of the live runs, and each of the 1,613 denials is checked as theorem. Repair targets the 252 denials caused by argument values, the kind that an edit of the call can fix; the others need tool from the agents own interface, an earlier step, the customers approval, or no call at all (Appendix H). For 88 of these 252 (34.9%), guard_repair? proves an admissible edit, in median of 2 ms per denial (at most 70 ms). Most of these repairs refund to the orders original payment method (64) or pay for flight change by card instead of travel certificate (18). The search ran after the episodes, so agents never received these repairs. The proved repairs nonetheless match the fixes of successful agents. When the agent itself later issued the repaired call, the task succeeded in 16 of 22 cases, against 7 of the other 66. For example, when Qwen3.5-0.8B requested payment of telecom bill that was not yet overdue, guard_repair? proved that requesting the customers overdue bill instead is admissible; with feedback, the agent made the same switch in another task with the same bills and succeeded.

sections.content: Agent guardrails and formal policy enforcement. Safeguards for tool-using language-model agents range from learned guard models to explicit runtime policy enforcement. Progent expresses least-privilege policies as symbolic constraints over tool calls (Shi et al., 2026); AgentSpec provides domain-specific language for specifying triggers, predicates, and runtime enforcement actions (Wang et al., 2026a); CaMeL separates trusted control flow from untrusted data and uses capabilities to restrict unauthorized information flows under prompt injection (Debenedetti et al., 2025); and FORGE specifies policies in Datalog and enforces them through reference monitor backed by an assumeguarantee contract on observable state (Palumbo et al., 2026). These systems extend longer formal-methods tradition in runtime shielding, in which monitor blocks or repairs actions that would violate formal safety specification (Könighofer et al., 2017; Alshiekh et al., 2017). Recent work has also begun applying Lean directly to agent behavior: the Lean-Agent Protocol checks proposed financial-agent actions against Lean 4 policy obligations before execution (Rashie and Rashi, 2026), whereas Lean4Agent formalizes agent workflows and execution trajectories and uses verification outcomes to revise workflows (Wang et al., 2026b). Unlike these systems, LEANGUARD proves its admission procedure correct against temporal-logic semantics and returns the violated rule to the agent so that it can recover. Shields can substitute safe action for an unsafe one; LEANGUARD instead searches for an edit of the agents own call that preserves the users intent and proves the edited call admissible. Complementary work trains safety into the agent itself, through synthetic risk data or reinforcement learning (Zhou et al., 2025; Sha et al., 2025), and Lean feedback already serves as reinforcement-learning signal for theorem proving (Xin et al., 2025; Kim and Yun, 2026). Benchmarks. τ -bench and τ 2-bench evaluate agents in stateful interactions with simulated users, domain tools, and explicit policies (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2026), as does ToolSandbox (Lu et al., 2025), while ToolEmu exposes high-stakes failures with emulated tools (Ruan et al., 2024). Security and safety benchmarks measure prompt injection and broader risks (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2024). We additionally measure what happens after denial, both when the model corrects its call and when Lean repairs it.

sections.content: LEANGUARD enforces agent policies at the tool boundary with decision procedure proved correct against temporal-logic semantics, and its denials tell the agent which obligation failed. On τ 2-bench, no call that the Lean policy forbids is executed, and with feedback task success does not change significantly; on DTap, tool-mediated attacks mostly fail. denied call can then be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the model fixes the call more often than after bare denial; with proof-guided repair, Lean computes the fix and proves it admissible without the model. sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: LEANGUARDs guarantee is relative to the reviewed formal specification and its trusted inputs. We formalize only the tool-enforceable subset of each natural-language policy, and the formalization was drafted with an LLM-based authoring aid and corrected by hand; errors or omissions in this step are not caught by the proofs. The guarantee also assumes that the domain adapter reports the environment faithfully and that every consequential tool call passes through the monitor, and it does not cover the conversion of free-form dialogue into consent records. LEANGUARD governs tool calls only, so harm carried by the response text is out of scope  (Table 21)  . The read-only DTap deployment overstates protection relative to policy that permits benign writes. Proof-guided repair was evaluated offline on replayed denials; the runtime does not yet call it, so we cannot measure the effect of delivering repair to the agent. Two τ 2-bench rules are stricter than the benchmarks policy. On DTap, our policies cover seven of the benchmarks 14 domains. Judge-flagged episodes on τ 2-bench come from an LLM judge that can be wrong and is also one of the evaluated models. All experiments use one model family (Qwen), English-language tasks, and simulated users.

sections.title: Lines of Lean
sections.content: Neurosymbolic reasoning and verification. complementary line of work uses symbolic methods to check and improve language-model reasoning. Proof of Thought translates structured model outputs into first-order logic for theorem-prover checking (Ganguly et al., 2024), while SequentProver trains agents to construct and revise executable SMT programs using solver feedback (Ganguly et al., 2026a). VERGE uses logical verification and error localization to guide iterative answer refinement (Singh et al., 2026a). The reliability of these methods also depends on the formalization: Grammars of Formal Uncertainty studies uncertainty in generated formal artifacts (Ganguly et al., 2025), and Beyond Solver Verdicts develops learned verifier for reference equivalence to detect incorrect translations that preserve solver verdicts (Singh et al., 2026b). Related work checks clinical reports against formalized findings and clinical knowledge (Singh et al., 2026c) and evaluates stochastic-process theorem proving in Lean (Davidovich et al., 2026). Broader studies examine inference-time reasoning strategies and their evaluation (Hariri et al., 2026), while Trust The Typical detects potentially unsafe inputs through deviations from the distribution of acceptable prompts (Ganguly et al., 2026b).
